items.title: Spleen: intraperitoneal organ most injured in blunt trauma
items.contentHtml:
Bazo: órgano intraperitoneal más lesionado en trauma contuso

El bazo es el órgano intraperitoneal más lesionado en el trauma abdominal contuso, seguido por el hígado. Su parénquima friable y su fijación ligamentosa lo hacen vulnerable a fuerzas de desaceleración y compresión. En trauma penetrante, el órgano más afectado es el hígado por su mayor superficie. La mortalidad por trauma esplénico aislado es baja si se maneja adecuadamente. La sospecha clínica debe ser alta en accidentes de tránsito con impacto lateral izquierdo o caídas de altura. La presencia de fracturas costales izquierdas inferiores (9ª-11ª) aumenta la probabilidad de lesión esplénica.

items.title: Mechanism of splenic injury in blunt trauma
items.contentHtml:
Mecanismo de lesión esplénica en trauma contuso

El mecanismo más frecuente es el trauma contuso abdominal, como accidentes de tráfico (impacto frontal o lateral), caídas desde altura, agresiones y accidentes deportivos. La compresión directa contra la columna vertebral o las costillas fracturadas produce laceración o estallido. La desaceleración brusca causa desgarros en los ligamentos esplénicos y lesión de la cápsula. En trauma contuso de alta energía, la lesión esplénica puede asociarse a otras lesiones intraabdominales (hígado, riñón, páncreas). La evaluación inicial incluye la ecografía enfocada en trauma (e-FAST) para detectar líquido libre, pero la tomografía computarizada con contraste es el estándar en pacientes hemodinámicamente estables.

items.title: Referred pain to the left shoulder: Kehr sign
items.contentHtml:
Pain referred to the left shoulder

Pain referred to the left shoulder is a classic symptom of diaphragmatic irritation due to intraperitoneal blood, known as Kehr's sign. It is caused by irritation of the left phrenic nerve (C3-C5 roots), which shares sensory territory with the shoulder. This sign is suggestive of splenic injury, but is not specific; It can also appear in subphrenic abscesses or pancreatitis. In trauma, its presence with hypotension forces us to suspect massive hemoperitoneum. Kehr's sign may be exacerbated by placing the patient in the Trendelenburg position. It is more useful in conscious patients without associated injuries that mask the pain.

items.title: Kehr sign: diagnostic value
items.contentHtml:
Suggestive Kehr's sign

The Kehr's sign is the presence of pain in the left shoulder, typically when lying down or with pressure in the left upper quadrant, due to irritation of the diaphragm by blood or gastrointestinal contents. In splenic trauma, it is a clinical finding that suggests high peritoneal irritation. However, his absence does not rule out injury. Its sensitivity is low, but its specificity is high when associated with other signs of peritoneal irritation. In the resident examination, it is asked as a classic finding of splenic rupture. The presence of Kehr's sign with hemodynamic instability indicates immediate surgical indication.

items.title: Hypotension and acute abdomen: hemorrhagic shock
items.contentHtml:
Hypotension with acute abdomen

Hypotension with signs of acute abdomen (pain, guarding, distension) in a patient with blunt trauma suggests massive hemoperitoneum, the most common cause being splenic injury. Blood loss may be rapid and not self-limiting. The initial response is resuscitation with crystalloid and blood, but if instability persists after resuscitation, emergency laparotomy is indicated. Trauma-focused ultrasound (e-FAST) can confirm free fluid in less than 5 minutes. Surgery should not be delayed to perform CT in unstable patients. Mortality increases if surgery is delayed more than 60 minutes in the presence of hypotension.

items.title: Contrast-enhanced tomography: diagnostic standard
items.contentHtml:
Contrast-enhanced tomography is standard

Computed tomography (CT) with intravenous contrast is the gold standard for evaluating splenic lesions in hemodynamically stable patients. It allows the injury to be classified according to the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) scale, based on findings such as laceration, subcapsular or vascular hematoma. CT identifies signs of active bleeding (contrast extravasation), pseudoaneurysms, and associated injuries. Sensitivity is >95% for splenic lesions. In the portal phase, parenchymal lesions are better detected. CT also guides the decision between nonoperative management, embolization, or surgery. In unstable patients, CT is contraindicated and laparotomy is performed.

items.title: Grade III with pseudoaneurysm: embolization
items.contentHtml:
Grade III with pseudoaneurysm: embolization

In splenic injuries grade III of the AAST scale (laceration with >3 cm depth or subcapsular hematoma >50% surface area or expansion), the presence of pseudoaneurysm or contrast extravasation on computed tomography indicates high risk of failure of non-operative management. Selective or superselective embolization of the splenic artery is the treatment of choice in hemodynamically stable patients, since it reduces the rate of splenectomy. It is performed through angiography and placement of coils or particles. If embolization is not available or fails, conservative surgery or splenectomy is performed. Proximal embolization decreases perfusion pressure, facilitating hemostasis.

items.title: Non-operative management: strict criteria
items.contentHtml:
Non-operative management in stable patients

Non-operative management is the standard treatment for splenic injuries in hemodynamically stable patients, without signs of peritoneal irritation, with computed tomography showing grade I to III injuries (sometimes IV without active bleeding). Requires monitoring in the intensive care unit, serial hemoglobin monitoring, and bed rest. The success rate is >90% in low grade injuries. It is contraindicated in patients with peritonitis, persistent hypotension or contrast extravasation. Advanced age (>55 years) was previously considered a relative contraindication, but today it can be attempted in selected patients. Follow-up imaging is only performed if there is clinical deterioration.

items.title: Splenectomy: indication in instability
items.contentHtml:
Splenectomy in hemodynamic instability

Splenectomy is indicated in patients with hemodynamic instability (systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg that does not respond to resuscitation) or with massive active bleeding. In these cases, emergency laparotomy is the priority, and total splenectomy is the quickest and most definitive procedure. Splenectomy is preferred over repair when there is hilar injury or massive destruction. Conservative surgery (splenorrhaphy) is reserved for limited lesions in stable patients. After splenectomy, antibiotic prophylaxis and vaccines should be administered. Operative mortality is low if bleeding is controlled in time. The decision is made based on the response to resuscitation, not just the degree of injury.

items.title: Postsplenectomy vaccines: scheme
items.contentHtml:
Post-splenectomy vaccines

After splenectomy, the patient is at risk of sepsis due to encapsulated bacteria, so vaccines against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Haemophilus influenzae type b should be administered. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) is administered initially, followed by polysaccharide (PPSV23) at least 8 weeks later. Meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MenACWY) and serogroup B vaccine (MenB) are indicated. The Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine is given in one dose if not received before. Ideally, they are vaccinated 2 weeks before elective surgery or 14 days after emergency splenectomy. Revaccination with PPSV23 is required at 5 years.

items.title: Postsplenectomy reactive thrombocytosis
items.contentHtml:
Post-splenectomy reactive thrombocytosis

Reactive thrombocytosis is a common finding after splenectomy, due to the loss of platelet sequestration and regulation function of the spleen. The platelet count usually rises in the first 10 days and can exceed 1,000,000/µL. It is generally transient and does not require specific treatment if it is asymptomatic. However, in patients at risk of thrombosis (history of thromboembolism, cancer), low-dose aspirin may be considered. Extreme thrombocytosis (>1,500,000/µL) can cause hemorrhage from acquired von Willebrand disease. The patient should be monitored during the first weeks. The thrombotic risk is low compared to essential thrombocythemia.

items.title: Asplenia syndrome: fulminant sepsis
items.contentHtml:
Asplenia syndrome: fulminant sepsis

The asplenia syndrome refers to the condition of patients without a functional spleen, who are at risk of fulminant sepsis postsplenectomy (overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis syndrome, OPSI). Fulminant sepsis is a medical emergency with high mortality, mainly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae type b. It presents with fever, chills, hypotension and disseminated intravascular coagulation, often without a clear infectious focus. Prevention includes vaccination, antibiotic prophylaxis (daily oral penicillin or amoxicillin), and patient education about seeking medical attention for any fever. In case of fever, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics should be administered immediately. Mortality can exceed 50% if not treated in time.
